put.1941.0.B6.text: Editorial clarification: continuity is required on the closed interval [0,1], ensuring that all displayed integrals are finite. The available historical transcriptions only specify continuity on (0,1); the added endpoint condition is explicit and is not certified as original examination wording.
put.1941.0.B6.reviewed_statement:
Let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Prove that
$$\int_0^1\int_x^1\int_x^y f(x)f(y)f(z)\,dz\,dy\,dx=\frac1{3!}\left(\int_0^1f(t)\,dt\right)^3.$$

put.1947.0.A2.text: Editorial clarification: the identically zero solution is listed separately, following the separate case in Scholes’ discussion. In the remaining case f(1)>0, so the displayed power is defined also at x=0.
put.1947.0.A2.reviewed_statement:
A continuous function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfies
$$f\left(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right)=f(x)f(y)$$
for all real $x,y$. Prove that either $f$ is identically zero, or $f(1)>0$ and
$$f(x)=[f(1)]^{x^2}\qquad\text{for every real }x.$$

put.1948.0.A6.text: Source convention: the real power-series identity in alternative (ii) is interpreted on |x|<1, its interval of convergence.
put.1948.0.A6.reviewed_statement:
Answer either (i) or (ii):
(i) A force acts on the element $ d s $ of a closed plane curve. The magnitude of this force is $ r^{-1} d s $ where $ r $ is the radius of curvature at the point considered, and the direction of the force is perpendicular to the curve; it points to the convex side. Show that the system of such forces acting on all elements of the curve keep it in equilibrium.

(ii) Show that
$$
x+\frac{2}{3} x^{3}+\frac{2}{3} \frac{4}{5} x^{5}+\frac{2}{3} \frac{4}{5} \frac{6}{7} x^{7}+\cdots=\frac{\arcsin x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}} .
$$

put.1949.0.A6.text: Source convention: at x=0 the quotient sin(x)/x is interpreted by its removable extension.
put.1949.0.A6.reviewed_statement:
Prove that for every real or complex $x$,
$$\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1+2\cos(2x/3^k)}{3}=\frac{\sin x}{x}.$$

put.1949.0.B6.text: Source convention: the perpendicular is the segment from O towards the tangent foot; its intersection on that side of O determines T(P). Choosing the opposite intersection would describe a different iteration.
put.1949.0.B6.reviewed_statement:
Let $ C $ be a closed convex curve with a continuously turning tangent and let $ O $ be a point inside $ C $. With each point $ P $ on $ C $ we associate the point $ T(P) $ on $ C $ which is defined as follows: Draw the tangent to $ C $ at $ P $ and from $ O $ drop the perpendicular to that tangent. $ T(P) $ is then the point at which this perpendicular intersects the curve $ C $.

Starting now with a point $ P_{0} $ on $ C $, we define points $ P_{n} $ by the formula $ P_{n}= $ $ T\left(P_{n-1}\right), n \geq 1 $. Prove that the points $ P_{n} $ approach a limit, and characterize those points which can be limits of sequences $ P_{n} $. (You may consider the facts that $ T $ is a continuous transformation and that a convex curve lies on one side of each of its tangents as not requiring proofs.)

put.1950.0.B3.text: Source convention: calendar probability is interpreted as relative frequency in the repeating 400-year Gregorian calendar cycle, not a uniform probability distribution on all positive integers.

put.1954.0.B3.text: Source notation: parentheses (a,b) are explicitly defined here to mean a closed interval; this historical convention is retained.
put.1954.0.B3.reviewed_statement: Let $ a $ and $ b $ denote real numbers such that $ a<b $. The symbol $ (a, b) $ will denote the closed interval with the end points $ a, b $. Let there be given a collection of closed intervals $ \left(a_{1}, b_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(a_{n}, b_{n}\right) $ such that any two of these closed intervals have at least one point in common. Prove that there exists then a point which is contained in every one of these intervals.

put.1955.0.A4.text: Source convention: the intersections counted are inside the circle, excluding the n selected endpoints, as made explicit by the secondary source.
put.1955.0.A4.reviewed_statement: On a circle, $ n $ points are selected and the chords joining them in pairs are drawn. Assuming that no three of these chords are concurrent (except at the endpoints), how many points of intersection are there?

put.1956.0.B5.text: Source convention: a triangle means a 3-cycle in the joining graph; a nonzero geometric area is not part of the graph assertion.
put.1956.0.B5.reviewed_statement: Consider a set of $ 2 n $ points in space, $ n>1 $. Suppose they are joined by at least $ n^{2}+1 $ segments. Show that at least one triangle is formed. Show that for each $ n $ it is possible to have $ 2 n $ points joined by $ n^{2} $ segments without any triangles being formed.

put.1956.0.B7.text: Editorial clarification: both polynomials are required to be nonconstant. Without this condition unequal constants other than 0 and -1 are counterexamples. The added restriction is mathematically necessary and is not certified as original examination wording.
put.1956.0.B7.reviewed_statement: Let $P(z)$ and $Q(z)$ be nonconstant polynomials with complex coefficients. Suppose they have the same set of zeros, possibly with different multiplicities. Suppose also that $P(z)+1$ and $Q(z)+1$ have the same set of zeros. Prove that $P(z)\equiv Q(z)$.

put.1957.0.A3.text: Editorial correction: k>1 is required for the strict inequality. The longer transcription says positive integer, which would include k=1 and give 0<0. The secondary source explicitly excludes that case.
put.1957.0.A3.reviewed_statement:
$ A $ and $ B $ are real numbers and $ k $ an integer greater than 1. Show that
$$
\left|\frac{\cos k B \cos A-\cos k A \cos B}{\cos B-\cos A}\right|<k^{2}-1
$$
whenever the left side is defined.

put.1958.1.A3.text: Source convention: successive random choices are independent and uniform on [0,1].
put.1958.1.A3.reviewed_statement: Real numbers are chosen at random from the interval $ (0 \leq x \leq 1) $. If after choosing the $ n $th number the sum of the numbers so chosen first exceeds 1 , show that the expected or average value for $ n $ is $ e $.

put.1958.1.A6.text: Source convention: a positive annual interest rate is assumed for a finite perpetuity investment.
put.1958.1.A6.reviewed_statement: What is the smallest amount that may be invested at interest rate $ i $, compounded annually, in order that one may withdraw 1 dollar at the end of the first year, 4 dollars at the end of the second year, $ \ldots, n^{2} $ dollars at the end of the $ n $th year, in perpetuity?

put.1958.1.B4.text: Source convention: the two points are independently uniform with respect to surface area.
put.1958.1.B4.reviewed_statement: What is the average straight line distance between two points on a sphere of radius $ 1 ? $

put.1958.2.B5.text: Source convention: successive turns have the same directed angle. The phrase if there is one retains the possible absence of a finite limiting point.
put.1958.2.B5.reviewed_statement: The lengths of successive segments of a broken line are represented by the successive terms of the harmonic progression $ 1,1 / 2,1 / 3, \ldots, 1 / n, \ldots $. Each segment makes with the preceding segment a given angle $ \theta $. What is the distance and what is the direction of the limiting point (if there is one) from the initial point of the first segment?

put.1959.0.B5.text: Historical source variant explained: +4 is retained from the longer examination transcription. Scholes explicitly reports that the original question printed +4 and that his version changes it to -4 to simplify arithmetic. Both define legitimate distinct questions; no sign correction is silently applied.
put.1959.0.B5.reviewed_statement:
Find the equation of the smallest sphere tangent to both lines
$$(x,y,z)=(t+1,2t+4,-3t+5),\qquad t\in\mathbb R,$$
$$(x,y,z)=(4s-12,-s+8,s+17),\qquad s\in\mathbb R.$$

put.1960.0.A6.text: Source convention: throws of the six-sided die are independent and each face has probability 1/6, as made explicit by the secondary version.
put.1960.0.A6.reviewed_statement: A player throwing a die scores as many points as on the top face of the die and is to play until his score reaches or passes a total $ n $. Denote by $ p(n) $ the probability of making exactly the total $ n $, and find the value of $ \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} p(n) $.

put.1961.0.B2.text: Source convention: both points are chosen independently and uniformly along the segment.
put.1961.0.B2.reviewed_statement: Let $ \alpha $ and $ \beta $ be given positive real numbers, with $ \alpha<\beta $. If two points are selected at random from a straight line segment of length $ \beta $, what is the probability that the distance between them is at least $ \alpha $ ?

put.1962.0.A2.text: Source convention: the geometric mean is the nonnegative square root and the stated averages must exist. No squared-equation variant is substituted.
put.1962.0.A2.reviewed_statement: Find every real-valued function $ f $ whose domain is an interval $ I $ (finite or infinite) having 0 as a left-hand endpoint, such that for every positive member $ x $ of $ I $ the average of $ f $ over the closed interval $ [0, x] $ is equal to the geometric mean of the numbers $ f(0) $ and $ f(x) $.

put.1962.0.B3.text: Source convention: region means an open region. Scholes makes openness explicit; the boundedness assertion fails for arbitrary non-open convex sets.
put.1962.0.B3.reviewed_statement: Let $ S $ be a convex region in the Euclidean plane containing the origin. Assume that every ray (that is, half-line) from the origin has at least one point outside $ S $. Prove that $ S $ is bounded. (A region in the plane is defined to be convex if and only if the line segment joining every pair of its points lies entirely within the region.)

put.1962.0.B6.text: Editorial correction: exactly 2n equality points are required, as specified by Scholes, to exclude constant functions. This is an edited formulation, not a claim about the exact printed examination wording.
put.1962.0.B6.reviewed_statement: Let $f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(a_k\sin kx+b_k\cos kx)$, where $n$ is a positive integer and $a_k,b_k$ are real constants. Suppose $|f(x)|\leq1$ for $0\leq x\leq2\pi$, and $|f(x)|=1$ at exactly $2n$ distinct points in $[0,2\pi)$. Show that $f(x)=\cos(nx+a)$ for some real constant $a$.

put.1964.0.B1.text: Editorial correction: the sequence consists of positive integers, as specified by the secondary source.
put.1964.0.B1.reviewed_statement:
Let $ u_{k}(k=1,2, \ldots) $ be a sequence of positive integers, and let $ V_{n} $ be the number of those which are less than or equal to $ n $. Show that if
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 1 / u_{k}<\infty
$$
then
$$
\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} V_{n} / n=0
$$
